newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Cash crisis threatens Russia's "cultural capital".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cash crisis threatens Russia's "cultural capital".

text.p: As Yuri Temirkanov conducted the St Petersburg Philharmonic through the rousing finale of Mussorgsky's "Pictures at an Exhibition" it was hard to believe the cultural life of Russia's second city is dying.

Yet that is precisely how Temirkanov, who is also principal conductor of London's Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, portrays the financial crisis that has hit St Petersburg, which claims that it, rather than Moscow, is Russia's "cultural capital".

"They're killing off our culture," Temirkanov told a news conference at the Philharmonic Hall as the city's cultural and artistic elite denounced dramatic, unplanned cuts in state funding for the arts. He announced a symbolic day's closure in November to raise awareness of their plight.

The movement has brought together theatres, orchestras, the Kirov opera and ballet troupes, libraries, music schools and the city's world-renowned art galleries. Officials have promised more money, but arts administrators remain sceptical.

Mikhail Piotrovsky, director of the Hermitage museum, said the pictures at his exhibition risk freezing this winter as the heating has been cut off in the Winter Palace, home to a vast collection of masterpieces and itself an architectural treasure.

The temperature in Russia's "northern capital" rarely rises much above zero for four months from November and many of the ornate 18th and 19th century buildings housing St Petersburg's artistic treasure are literally falling apart for lack of funds.

But the culture ministry admits it has had less than a third of this year's promised budget from the finance ministry, and the arts in Russia are suffering like never before since the collapse of the Soviet Union robbed them of big state subsidies.

"Culture is under a terrible threat, from the leading cultural centres to the smallest, farthest flung village libraries," Alexander Solzhenitsyn, the Nobel Prize-winning writer and doyen of Soviet dissidents, told Reuters.
Closing the Hermitage, a national and world treasure on a par with Paris's Louvre, is abhorrent to Piotrovsky, whose father ran the gallery for decades before him.

Even during the 1941-43 German siege of what was then Leningrad, when more than half a million starved or froze to death, the Hermitage stayed open. For the enlightenment of troops on leave, guides described works which had been taken away for safety.
"We'll do all we can to avoid closing, it's our duty," Piotrovsky told Reuters. "If we have no heating, if our staff aren't being paid, we have to fight and lobby the government."
The Hermitage has received none of this year's budgeted $10 million for capital spending and only 19 percent of a similar amount promised by the state for wages and running costs.

Piotrovsky reckons the Hermitage, which earns about $2.5 million a year from its own efforts and donations, must follow the lead of western galleries in improving its takings. It is introducing new services aimed at foreign visitors, who already must pay many times the entrance fee charged to Russians.
Other institutions may be more at risk.

Vladimir Gusev, director of the less famous Russian Museum, housing the cream of domestic art from mediaeval icons to Socialist Realism, has been quoted as saying he may have to close altogether soon for lack of funds.
In some of the gallery's unheated rooms, damp is destroying neoclassical mouldings and plasterwork and works kept in the basements are being threatened by poor storage conditions.
Yet Piotrovsky's reluctance to use the ultimate threat of closure is matched elsewhere, sometimes through idealism, but also through a realistic assessment of the balance of power.

At the Philharmonic, which has had about 37 percent of its budgeted subsidy, director Anton Getman remarked: "We can threaten the government. But while miners can throw down their shovels and power workers can bring the country to a standstill, we cannot inflict material damage on the government.
"We could threaten to close down. But then what? That might suit the government. Once we shut down, we may not find it too easy to open again," he said.

Although tickets at the Philharmonic, costing $3 for a big performance like Temirkanov conducting Mussorgsky and Prokofiev, are a fraction of those in the West, they still help provide the average musician with about $100 a month.
That is close to the Russian average wage and not something orchestra players want to miss out on, although many of the country's bigger stars earn much more working or touring abroad.
Many state-funded Russian workers, including the armed forces, have not been paid for months or are on half-pay or less because of deep government financing problems.

President Boris Yeltsin, re-elected in July on a platform that included an end to wage arrears and improved funding for the arts, this month blamed big business tax dodgers for the problems and launched a special body to hunt the missing cash.
But the fear of many in Russia's once cosseted artistic elite is that a state run on free market principles will, as in some Western countries, neglect the arts even if times improve.
"We have imported many ideas from the West, unfortunately many of them bad ones," said Piotrovsky, noting the run-down of arts funding in many Western states over the past decade.
"It's not just the lack of cash," he said. "We feel that the state does not understand the importance of culture for Russia. I think it's more important than the economy.
"To support the economy we can get foreign money...But foreigners can't produce Russian culture."
